chapter.title: Lying on the bed: floating

cards.body: A bed holds you up without you doing anything. You lie down, you let go, and the bed does the rest. Water is the same bed. Floating is not a skill you add; it is what happens when you stop fighting the water and let it hold you.

cards.title: Your lungs are the float
cards.body:
A chest full of air floats. It works like a sealed bottle: push it under, and it comes back up. When you take a big breath in and hold it, your chest becomes that bottle.

This is why floating starts with a breath, not a movement. Breathe in deep, keep the air in, and your chest will rise to the surface on its own.

The rest of your body hangs off that chest. Your legs are heavy and will sink a little. That is normal. Hips a bit lower than the chest is still a float.

On your back, the water should cover your ears. If your ears are dry, your head is lifted, and a lifted head pushes your hips down. Chin up, ears in, and look at the ceiling.

Your hands do one small job: palms up, out to the sides, fingers open. Keep them under the water. Hands out of the water are weight on the wrong side of the bed.

cards.prompt: You lie back, and your hips keep sinking. From what you have read, what is the most likely cause?

options.text: You are not kicking hard enough
Your head is lifted and your ears are out of the water
You have too much air in your lungs

whyNot.a: That's kicking, not floating: a float is still, and legs hanging a little low is normal.
whyNot.c: That's backwards: a full chest is the float. More air lifts you, not sinks you.

cards.reteach: Think of a seesaw. Your head is one end, your hips the other. Lift the head and the hips go down. Lay the head back until your ears are under, and the hips come up.

cards.title: Back float at the wall, 30 seconds
cards.body: Stand in chest-deep water with your back to the wall and one hand on the edge behind you. Take a deep breath in and hold it. Lean back until your ears go under and your eyes see the ceiling. Let your legs drift up, keep the hand on the wall, and count to 10. Next try, let the hand go for 5 seconds, then put it back. Then 15. Then 30, with no hands at all.

cards.title: Front float, and getting back up
cards.body:
The front float is the same idea, face down. Hold the wall with both hands, breathe in, put your face in the water, and let your legs lift behind you. Breathe out slowly through your nose like in chapter 2. You will sink a little as the air leaves; that is fine for 10 seconds.

First do it holding the wall. Then let one hand go. Then both. Count to 10 and stand up.

Standing up from a back float is the same move as chapter 1 in reverse order. Tuck your knees to your chest, press your arms forward and down, and your body rolls upright. Feet find the floor.

From a front float: knees in, hands press down, head comes up, feet down. Do it slowly the first few times. Rushing is what makes you swallow water.

cards.prompt: You are floating on your back, and you feel yourself start to tilt and sink. What do you do?

options.text: Breathe out and kick your legs to stay up
Lift your head to see where the wall is
Keep the air in, lay your head back, and if it still sinks, tuck your knees and stand

whyNot.a: That's letting the air out, not holding it: breathing out empties the float and you sink faster.
whyNot.b: That's the seesaw problem: lifting your head pushes your hips down and makes the sink worse.

cards.reteach: Two things fix a sinking float: keep the air in and drop the head back. If neither works in a second or two, there is nothing to save. Tuck, press down, stand. You are in chest-deep water.

cards.body: The big mistake is holding your head up to keep your face dry. It feels safer. It is the opposite: your head is heavy, and holding it up drags your hips and legs down. You can spot it in yourself when your ears are dry and your neck is tense. Ears in, neck loose, chin to the ceiling.

cards.prompt: What keeps your chest at the surface when you float?

options.text: A lungful of air that you hold in
Moving your arms in small circles
Pressing your hands down on the water

whyNot.b: That's treading water, later in the handbook, not floating. A float is still.
whyNot.c: That's the move for standing up, not floating. Pressing down brings your body upright.

cards.reteach: Your chest full of air is a sealed bottle. It floats on its own. Breathe in, hold, lie back, and let it do the work. Nothing else is needed.

cards.body: Tonight in a bath: lie back, breathe in deep, ears under, hands palm up. Feel your chest lift. Let the air out and feel it drop.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now float on your back for 30 seconds and on your front for 10 seconds with no hands on anything, and return to standing calmly from both.
